131: Work can protect or weaken mental health. Why this matters, and what organisations can do.
137: Video: Prevalence of mental health problems in Portugal
138: CC English subtitles to be added in the final version.
139: Prevalence of mental health problems in Portugal
140: Portugal has a high prevalence of anxiety and depression among the adult population.
141: Many cases do not receive adequate clinical or psychological support.
142: Psychological distress is often invisible and unrecognised.
143: Work can act as a protective factor or a risk factor for mental health.
144: The way work is organised directly affects wellbeing.
148: Mental health is the ability to cope with challenges, to work and to contribute to the community.
149: Wellbeing involves emotional balance, satisfaction and a sense of purpose.
150: At work, it translates into feeling valued, safe and competent.
151: Mental health is dynamic and varies over time and with context.
152: The work context directly influences mental health.
155: Video: The role of organisations in promoting mental health
156: The role of organisations in promoting mental health
157: Organisations have a central role in promoting their employees’ mental health.
158: The workplace is often where signs of psychological distress first appear.
159: Attentive environments make it possible to identify and respond to distress earlier.
160: Prevention, through healthy organisational cultures, is essential.
161: Environments with respect, fairness, support and balance promote wellbeing and performance.
165: In each example, the same kind of demand can protect or weaken mental health. The difference lies in how the context responds.
166: Ana and Rita have similar roles and an equally intense period of work.
168: She has the autonomy to organise her tasks, feels her effort is recognised and knows she can ask for help. She ends the period tired, but with a sense of achievement.
170: She works under constant pressure, with no room for decisions and afraid of making mistakes. The same tiredness turns into exhaustion.
172: The differenceThe demand is similar. What changes is autonomy, support and recognition.
176: An employee who is usually participative starts to withdraw, misses meetings and responds irritably.
178: The line manager notices the change, approaches without judging and makes room to talk. The distress is recognised in time.
180: The same behaviour is read as “lack of commitment”. The distress stays invisible and gets worse.
181: The differenceThe first signs of distress often appear at work. Recognising them depends on someone being attentive.
182: Coming back after a difficult period
185: After sick leave for mental health reasons, an employee returns to the team.
187: With listening, gradual adjustment of tasks and no stigma, the reintegration goes well and builds confidence.
189: As if nothing had happened, the person feels exposed and the risk of relapse increases.
190: The differenceCaring for mental health is not just avoiding the crisis. It means supporting people before, during and after.
193: Work can protect or weaken mental health. The difference is rarely in the task itself, but in the autonomy, support, recognition and attention that the organisation gives people.

203: Identify, observe and act on the aspects of work that can affect physical, emotional and social health.
209: Risks that are not always visible
210: Psychosocial risks are aspects of work that can negatively affect physical, emotional and social health.
211: They can be present in workload, leadership, relationships, organisational culture or the balance between professional and personal life. Although they are not always visible, their effects build up and can compromise wellbeing, performance and staying in work.
